title: The Effect of Hint Strength on the Benefits of Retrieval Practice https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/acp.3929 https://tipsforteachers.co.uk/research-the-effect-of-hint-strength-on-the-benefits-of-retrieval-practice/
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), November 28, 2024 — original paper:
summary: Barton summarises Vaughn and colleagues' two-experiment study into how the strength of hints given during retrieval practice affects real learning. Students recalling bone structures with strong hints recalled faster in the moment, but performed worse on a final test than those given weak or no hints, despite rating the strong-hint condition as more enjoyable and more effective. A second experiment using a criterion-learning design, requiring correct recall before moving on, did not remove this effect: strong hints still hurt final performance even when initial success was equalised. Barton draws the clear implication that students systematically misjudge which form of retrieval feels most productive, and that real-world familiar material may make this illusion worse. He argues teachers should favour weaker hints or no hints at all, and should explicitly teach students why easier-feeling retrieval practice can be the less effective kind.
points: Stronger hints during retrieval practice speed up initial recall but produce worse performance on a later test — a genuine desirable-difficulty trade-off.
Students consistently rate strong-hint retrieval as more enjoyable and more effective, even when it demonstrably harms their final performance.
A criterion-learning design (ensuring equal initial success) did not neutralise the negative effect of strong hints, ruling out unequal early success as the explanation.
Familiar, real-world material may make the strong-hint illusion worse, so teachers should be especially cautious with hints on content students partly already know.
quotes: Stronger hints, while leading to faster initial recall, resulted in poorer final performance, yet participants paradoxically rated strong hints as more enjoyable and effective.
Retrieval practice is beneficial, but the strength of hints used should be carefully considered.
Students may not be aware of the negative impact of strong hints on their learning.
Real-world learning materials may be more susceptible to the negative effects of strong hints.
A criterion-learning paradigm does not necessarily mitigate the negative effects of strong hints.
Although retrieval practice is a beneficial study strategy, students learning real-world course material might want to avoid testing with hints, especially strong hints.
